newsitem.title: USA: El Nino drought seen raising interest in US soyoil.
newsitem.headline: El Nino drought seen raising interest in US soyoil.

text.p: Soybean oil could become a hot commodity next year as the strongest El Nino since 1983 threatens to cut world oilseed production, analysts said.
"We're going to go into a two-year bull market starting in about six months," said Ann Frick, oilseed analyst with Prudential Securities.

Frick predicted soyoil futures at the Chicago Board of Trade would peak at 28.00 cents per pound during the 1997/98 (Sept/Aug) soybean crop year and could go even higher the next year. December soyoil closed at 22.74 cents on Tuesday.

Warm ocean temperatures off the west coast of South America have triggered the El Nino global weather pattern, and the phenomenon is strengthening, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration said on June 10.

The effect has been associated with droughts in the southern hemisphere. The worst El Nino this century hit in 1982-83 and caused billions of dollars in crop damage, with Indonesia, Australia and the Philippines bearing the brunt.
Crop producing regions from India to Australia are already feeling the effects of dry weather tied to the current El Nino, analysts said.
"We are seeing dryness in parts of Asia and Australia and they're beginning to attribute the drought to El Nino," said Mike Helmar, senior economist at the WEFA Group.

"We're likely to see a continued pattern of dryness into next year," Helmar said. "Not only are we looking at potential increases in demand for soyoil but we're also looking at the potential for some dramatic reductions in soybean crops next year."
Edible oils are customarily in huge demand in China, India, Indonesia and other Asian countries where they are used daily as cooking oils with rice and other grain-based dishes.

Analysts cautioned that the bull run in soyoil would not start until demand soaked up current massive U.S. soyoil stockpiles. The U.S. Census Bureau last month put U.S. soyoil supplies at more than two billion pounds.
World demand for soymeal this year has far outstripped soyoil usage. U.S. processors have been crushing soybeans at a record pace to meet that demand, leaving soyoil supplies high.

"The biggest problem is we're crushing like gangbusters," said Dean Witter analyst Jerry Gidel. "My short-term attitude is that soyoil is reasonably priced, but I sense that we are going to have less competition from the tropicals next year."
Gidel said El Nino-related dryness could cut palm oil production in Malaysia and Indonesia next year and also threaten cottonseed and peanut crops in China and India.
"China is the major wild card in this," he said. "How much impact has this drought had on soybeans, cottonseed and peanuts? Will they try to buy bean oil or will they come in and buy beans?"

Crops elsewhere may not be safe from Mother Nature either in coming months. El Nino effects have been linked to flooding in southern Brazil and Argentina during those countries' growing season, which could cut grain and oilseed production.
The U.S. Agriculture Department has predicted the two countries would produce roughly 42 million tonnes of soybeans next year.

While the Department has also predicted U.S. farmers will produce a record soybean crop this year, oil content may be below normal, analysts said. The National Weather Service has predicted below normal temperatures during September in key U.S. soybean growing areas, which has prompted concerns of an early freeze.

"What normally happens is if the plant is prematurely killed, the protein will tend to be elevated a little and the oil content is decreased a little," Purdue University agronomist Ellsworth Christmas said.

"You will get green beans if the freeze comes really early," he said. "That probably reduces the oil content some, but you're going to also end up with green oil and an oil that has a shorter shelf life. The quality is reduced as well as the quantity."
((Chicago Newsdesk 312-408-8720))
